mcqs.question: Why is a TLB lookup dramatically faster than a page table walk, even though both ultimately produce a translation?
options: The TLB is implemented as a small, fast on-chip hardware cache checked before any walk is attempted, versus a walk that requires multiple accesses to memory
The TLB stores compressed page tables that are smaller to search
TLB lookups skip permission checking entirely
The page table walk always requires a full flush of the TLB first
mcqs.explanation: The TLB's speed comes from being small, on-chip hardware searched in parallel, versus a walk that has to touch memory once per page table level. It isn't a compressed page table, doesn't skip permission checks, and a walk doesn't require flushing the TLB first.

mcqs.question: TLB hit ratio drops from 99% to 95%, with a 1-cycle hit and 400-cycle miss cost. What happens to average translation time?
options: It stays roughly the same, since 95% still sounds high
It increases slightly, by about 1 cycle
It roughly quadruples, from about 5 cycles to about 21 cycles
It becomes 400 cycles for every access
mcqs.explanation: At 99%: 0.99(1) + 0.01(401) ≈ 5 cycles. At 95%: 0.95(1) + 0.05(401) ≈ 21 cycles — roughly a 4x increase, because misses are so much more expensive than hits that even a small ratio drop compounds heavily. It's not unchanged, not a tiny 1-cycle bump, and not every access paying the full miss cost.

mcqs.question: Without ASID tagging, why does flushing the TLB on a context switch hurt performance beyond the flush operation itself?
options: The flush operation itself takes hundreds of milliseconds
Flushing corrupts the page table permanently
The newly-scheduled process starts with an empty TLB and pays full page-table-walk cost on its first accesses to each page, until it re-warms
The next process cannot run until an entirely new page table is built from scratch
mcqs.explanation: The flush itself is cheap; the real cost is the newly-scheduled process running cold, missing on translations it would otherwise have cached, until enough accesses rebuild TLB coverage. The flush doesn't corrupt the page table or take hundreds of milliseconds, and no new page table needs to be built.

mcqs.question: How do ASIDs (PCIDs) reduce the TLB cost of context switching?
options: They tag TLB entries with an address-space identifier, so multiple processes' translations can coexist and a quick switch back doesn't require starting cold
They eliminate the need for a TLB entirely
They make every page table walk instantaneous
They force every process to share the same virtual address mappings
mcqs.explanation: ASIDs let entries from multiple address spaces coexist in the TLB simultaneously, so switching back to a recently-run process can hit on entries that were never evicted, instead of requiring a full flush. They don't remove the TLB, don't make walks instant, and processes keep their own distinct mappings.

mcqs.question: A workload with many short-lived threads shows elevated average memory latency, but the scheduler's own routines account for very little measured time. What's a likely explanation?
options: The scheduler must be buggy
Frequent context switches without ASID support are cold-starting the TLB repeatedly, and the re-warming cost shows up as memory latency in the newly-scheduled process, not as scheduler time
This can only be explained by a hardware fault
This pattern is unrelated to context switching frequency
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the indirect TLB-churn cost: the visible time in the scheduler routine is small, but the following process pays elevated latency from repeated cold-TLB page-table walks. It isn't necessarily a scheduler bug or hardware fault, and it's very much tied to switching frequency.
